headline: Five EU Nations Announce Rwanda 'Return Hub,' Reviving Britain's £700m Greatest Hit
subheadline: *Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have adopted the one British policy so successful that Britain spent £700 million on it before quietly pretending it never happened.*
author: Henrik Baumann, Continental Affairs Desk
seoTitle: EU Revives Britain's £700m Rwanda Deportation Plan
seoDescription: Satire: Five EU countries plan a migrant 'return hub' in Rwanda, adopting the British policy that cost £700m and deported almost nobody.
sourceEvent: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a joint 'return hub' in Rwanda for failed asylum seekers, according to the BBC. The plan echoes the UK's abandoned Rwanda deportation scheme, which cost over £700 million and was scrapped after years of legal challenges.

altHeadlines: Europe Acquires Britain's £700m Deportation Scheme, Still in Original Packaging
EU Nations License UK Policy That Deported Fewer People Than It Employed Ministers

body:
BRUSSELS — Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a joint migrant "return hub" in Rwanda this week, boldly adopting the one British policy so successful that Britain spent £700 million on it before quietly pretending it had never happened.

The plan would see failed asylum seekers processed at a centre in Kigali — a concept British officials pioneered in 2022 and then perfected over two years, multiple court rulings and almost zero involuntary deportations, a track record one EU diplomat described as "the gold standard of theoretical deterrence."

A spokesperson for the five-nation coalition said the group had been "hugely impressed" by the British model, particularly the part where nobody went anywhere. "The genius is in what it doesn't do," the spokesperson said. "Britain built a deterrence so powerful it deterred its own government from using it. We felt Europe deserved that kind of ambition."

Under the terms of the arrangement, the policy will be transferred to the continent in its original packaging, accompanied by several complimentary rulings from the UK Supreme Court declaring key components of it unlawful, which officials described as "collector's items." Britain has also reportedly offered, at cost, a warehouse of unused chartered-flight vouchers and one commemorative deportation bib, never worn.

"People ask why you'd acquire a policy that deported fewer people than it employed ministers," said one senior analyst who has tracked the scheme since its inception. "But you have to think of it as software. Britain spent £700 million on the beta. Europe is simply shipping version 1.0, and this time it might have a user."

Sources say Rwanda has welcomed the deal, having now signed multiple agreements to host Europe's asylum-processing ambitions — a diplomatic record known in Kigali as "the hat trick." A Rwandan official familiar with the negotiations said the country was "honoured to once again serve as the venue where European ideas about Europe get resolved."

Reaction in Britain was mixed. Westminster sources described a mood of "quiet vindication," with one former adviser noting it was "gratifying to watch the continent finally catch up to a policy we abandoned for being too expensive, too unlawful and too theoretical." The UK government declined to comment, reportedly on the grounds that it is still paying for the scheme and would prefer not to discuss the scheme.

Critics warned the plan could face the same legal obstacles, political backlash and fundamental logistical implausibility as the original — a concern coalition officials dismissed as "fear-mongering by people who have read the policy."

At press time, the five nations were reportedly in negotiations to license Britain's entire back catalogue of deterrence, including a £37 billion test-and-trace system and a Home Office spreadsheet that misplaced thousands of asylum cases in what was described internally as "a formatting issue."
